title: A British Party Got a Huge Gift. Is It Fair?
summary:
Imagine your friend got a giant bag of candy — £72 million worth. That's what happened to a British political party called Reform UK. Two rich businessmen, Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, each gave £36 million. That's one of the biggest donations in British history.

But here's the twist: both men are British, but they lived abroad until recently. The government is worried that people who don't live in the UK are influencing British politics. So they want to pass a new rule: anyone living overseas can only donate up to £100,000 a year. And they want the rule to count from March 25, 2026 — even for money already given.

Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform UK, says the donations are "100% compliant with the law today." He's angry about the idea of making the rule go back in time. He says if the government does that, he'll try to stop trade unions from donating to other parties. Trade unions are groups that collect money from workers to help them.

Paul Nowak, a trade union leader, says that's not the same. He says there's a big difference between "care workers chipping in a few quid a year" and "a party bought and paid for by billionaires." The debate is happening right now in Parliament.
why_it_matters: You will grow up seeing money and politics mixed together, so it helps to ask who paid for the messages you see and whether the rules are the same for everyone.

background_read: Reform UK (a British political party led by Nigel Farage) is fairly new, and it grew out of the campaign to take Britain out of the European Union.
In Britain, political parties are mostly paid for by private donations, and a group called the Electoral Commission keeps track of who gives money to whom.
Parliament (the place in London where British laws are made) is debating this new donation rule right now.
Article_Structure: WHO: Reform UK and its leader Nigel Farage received £36 million each from businessmen Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne; the government and trade union leader Paul Nowak are pushing back.
WHAT: The government wants a new rule that anyone living overseas can donate only up to £100,000 a year, counting from March 25, 2026.
WHERE: In Britain, with the debate happening right now in Parliament.

WHY: The government worries that people who live abroad are influencing British politics, while Farage says the donations are 100% compliant with the law today and calls a rule that looks backward unfair.

perspectives.description: It worries that people who live outside Britain should not have so much power over British politics, so it wants a £100,000 yearly limit on overseas donations.
They say the money was given legally and that changing the rule to count money already donated is unfair; Farage even threatens to go after trade union donations to other parties.
Paul Nowak says workers giving a few pounds a year is completely different from a party being bought and paid for by billionaires.
